      "source_page": 78,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nrunning on multiple processor cores. The order in which the threads access such data\nwill affect the result, which makes it non-deterministic (race condition).\nA fully deterministic calculation must be designed, implemented and integrated in a\nway such that it is independent of processor load caused by other functions and cal-\nculations, sporadic unrelated events, race conditions, deviating random numbers etc.,\ni.e. for the same input and initial conditions it always produces the same result within\na given time.\n7.6.2 Deterministic Client\nAs explained in 7.6.1, future systems need high computing performance in combina-\ntion with high ASIL safety goals. In this chapter we specify mechanisms which support\ndeterministic multithread execution to support high performance software lockstep so-\nlutions. Here are some additional rationales behind it:\n•\nSafety goals for Highly Automated Driving (HAD) systems can be up to ASIL D.\n•\nHigh Performance Computing (HPC) demands can only be met by non\nautomotive-grade, e.g. consumer electronics (CE), microprocessors, which have\nhigh transient hardware error rates compared to automotive-grade microcon-\ntrollers. Most likely no such microprocessor is available for ASIL above B, at\nleast for the parts relevant to the design.\n•\nTo deal with high error rates, ASIL C/D HAD applications require specific mea-\nsures, in particular software lockstep, where execution is done redundantly\nthrough two different paths and the result is compared to detect errors.\n•\nTo make these redundant calculations comparable, software lockstep requires a\nfully deterministic calculation as defined in 7.6.1.3.\n•\nTo meet HPC demands, highly predictable and reliable multi-threading must be\nsupported\nTwo redundant\nprocesses\n, which run in an internal cycle, get in each cycle the same\ninput data via regular interfaces of\nCommunication Management\nand produce (in\nthe absence of errors) the same results, due to full deterministic execution.\nExecution Management\nprovides\nDeterministicClient\nAPIs to support control\nof the process-internal cycle, a deterministic worker pool, activation time stamps and\nrandom numbers. In case of multiple\nprocesses\nfor redundant execution, the\nDeter-\nministicClient\ninteracts with a\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nto ensure identical\nbehavior of the redundantly executed\nprocesses\n.\nThe activation time stamps are provided by local time sychronization slave or mas-\nter, and the redundant executions between the\nprocesses\nare handled by the corre-\nsponding\nDeterministicSyncMaster\n, which propagates the activation time stamp\n78 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_document": "AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement",
      "source_page": 79,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nand the calculated cycle information for next execution to all the connected\nDeter-\nministicClient\n. The calculated data of the application\nprocesses\nis published\nthrough\nCommunication Management\n.\nFor each execution cycle, the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nsynchronizes the\nDe-\nterministicClient\ns. It makes sure that random numbers and activation time\nstamps that are sent to\nDeterministicClient\ns are identical for the redundantly ex-\necution. The\nDeterministicClient\ns then synchronize the triggering of execution\nbased on the received activation time stamps. An optional software lockstep framework\nmay subscribe to the output of the redundant\nprocesses\nand compare the output to\ndetect failures (e.g. transient processor core or memory errors due to radiation) in\none of the redundant\nprocesses\n. This infrastructure layer can span over multiple\nhardware instances and is implementation specific.\nThe\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\nneeds to provide some library functions to sup-\nport redundant deterministic execution with sufficient isolation. The library functions\n(\nDeterministicClient\n) run in the context of the user\nprocess\n. Figure 7.16 con-\nsiders how\nDeterministicClient\ncan be used in one of the redundantly executed\nprocesses\n."

Within a\nprocess\n, all input data is available via ara::com (polling-based access only) when\nexecution starts and is stable over one execution cycle. For details see 7.6.3.1.\nThe workload can be deployed to a worker pool API, which allows deterministic execu-\ntion of a set of container elements (e.g. data sets), which are processed in parallel by\nthe same runnable object (i.e. application function). The runnable object is not allowed\nto exchange any information while it is running, i.e. it doesn't access data which can be\naltered by other instances of the runnable object to avoid race conditions. The runnable\nobject instances can physically run in parallel or sequentially in any order. For details\nsee 7.6.3.2.\nAdditional\nDeterministicClient\nAPIs provide random numbers and activation time\nstamps. Common HAD algorithms use particle filters which require random numbers.\nIf used from within the worker pool, the random numbers are assigned to specific con-\ntainer elements to allow deterministic redundant execution. The activation time stamps\ndon't change until the\nprocess\nreaches its next wait point. For deterministic redun-\ndant execution, random number seeds and time stamps need to be synchronized. For\ndetails see 7.6.3.3 and 7.6.3.4.\nAt the end of the execution cycle, the\nprocess\nreturns to the wait point and waits for\nthe next activation.\nThe APIs of\nDeterministicClient\nare standardized and provide abstraction of the\napplication deployment on the actual hardware. The implementation is vendor specific\nand needs to be configured at integration time individually for each\nprocess\nwhich\nuses it.\nThe\nDeterministicClient\nClass is only local to the\nprocess\n. Therefore, there is\ncurrently no security concern foreseen for this API.\nDifferent variants of the\nDeterministicClient\nmight work in a software lockstep\nenvironment or stand-alone, to support cyclic execution and deterministic worker pools.\n[SWS_EM_02551]\n{OBSOLETE}\nMissing DeterministicClient\n⌈\nIf the configuration of\nDeterministicClient\nis missing then\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::\nWaitForActivation\nshall return Error\nkFailed\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00053)\n80 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.17: Deterministic Execution Interface\n7.6.3 Cyclic Deterministic Execution\nThis section describes the APIs shown in Figure 7.16, and how they need to be used\nby a\nprocess\nto execute deterministically, so the\nprocess\ncan be transparently inte-\ngrated into a software lockstep environment.\n7.6.3.1 Control of Cyclic Execution\nExecution Management\nprovides an API to trigger and control recurring, i.e. cyclic\nexecution of the main thread code within a\nprocess\n.\n[SWS_EM_01301]\n{OBSOLETE}\nCyclic Execution\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall\nprovide a blocking wait point API\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::Wait-\nForActivation\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00052, RS_EM_00113)\nAfter the\nprocess\nhas been started by\nExecution Management\n, it reports\nara::\nexec::ExecutionState kRunning\n(see 7.4.1) and calls\nara::exec::Deter-\nministicClient::WaitForActivation\n.\n81 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nThe\nprocess\nexecutes one cycle when\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::\nWaitForActivation\nreturns and then calls the API again to wait for the next activa-\ntion.\nA return value controls the internal lifecycle (e.g. init, run, terminate) of the\nprocess\n,\nsee Figure 7.16. The return codes are used to synchronize the behavior of two\npro-\ncesses\nin case they are executed redundantly.\n[SWS_EM_01302]\n{OBSOLETE}\nCyclic Execution Control\n⌈\nara::exec::Deter-\nministicClient::WaitForActivation\nshall return a code to control the execu-\ntion mode of the calling\nprocess\n. Possible codes are\nkRegisterServices\n,\nkSer-\nviceDiscovery\n,\nkInit\n,\nkRun\n, and\nkTerminate\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00052)\nThe\nara::exec::ActivationReturnType\n(see [SWS_EM_02201]) returned from\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\ndetermines the ac-\ntions taken at each cycle:\n•\nkRegisterServices\n The\nprocess\nregisters its communication services, i.e.\nthe services it offers via\nCommunication Management\n. This should be the\nonly occasion for performing service registering. No other functionality should be\nperformed in this step to limit resource consumption and runtime, so no dedicated\nbudget needs to be assigned.\n•\nkServiceDiscovery\n The\nprocess\ndoes communication service discovery.\nThis should be the only occasion for performing service discovery, except a ser-\nvice needs to be replaced later (see ([SWS_EM_01304]). No other functionality\nshould be performed in this step to limit resource consumption and runtime, so\nno dedicated budget needs to be assigned.\n•\nkInit\n The\nprocess\ninitializes its internal data structures. The worker pool\n(see 7.6.3.2) can be accessed once or several time sequentially. A budget (see\n7.6.3.5) needs to be assigned to the Init cycle.\n•\nkRun\n The\nprocess\nperforms one cycle of its normal cyclic execution. This can\nbe repeated indefinitely. The worker pool (see 7.6.3.2) can be accessed once\nor several times sequentially within a cycle. A budget (see 7.6.3.5) needs to be\nassigned.\n•\nkTerminate\n The deterministic client prepares to terminate. It is up to the\nprocess\nwhether this also leads to the actual termination of the\nprocess\nand\nif so the actual termination is performed according to [SWS_EM_01404], see\nSection 7.4.2.\n[SWS_EM_01303]\n{OBSOLETE}\nCyclic Execution Control Sequence\n⌈\nThe return\ncode of\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\nshall follow\nthis sequence:\nkRegisterServices\n,\nkServiceDiscovery\n,\nkInit\n,\nkRun\n, and\nkTerminate\n. Note that\nkRun\nis expected to be returned multiple times.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00052)\n[SWS_EM_01304]\n{OBSOLETE}\nService Modification\n⌈\nIn case a service which is ac-\ncessed by the\nprocess\nneeds to be replaced (e.g. due to unavailability) while the\n82 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nNote that with respect to [SWS_EM_01352], the deterministic client used by the Ap-\nplication detects the\ncycleTimeValue\noverrun and reports it to the application.       "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.18: Worker Pool Usage\nIf the number of required container elements exceeds the number of workers (threads)\nin the deterministic worker pool,\nExecution Management\ncan use the worker pool\nseveral times sequentially (with unrestricted interleaving), which shall be transparent\nto the user of the worker pool.\nTo achieve Data Determinism, the parallel workers need to satisfy certain implemen-\ntation properties, e.g. no exchange of data is allowed between the instances of the\nrunnable object which are processed by the workers. For details see [10]. Other, more\ncomplex solutions which allow interaction between the workers would be possible, but\nthey increase complexity, reduce utilization and transparency, and are error-prone re-\ngarding the deterministic behavior.\nThe worker pool runs within the\nprocess\ncontext of the caller of this API. It is de-\nsigned as part of\nExecution Management\nto guarantee the deterministic behavior\nby incorporating it in the\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActi-\nvation\ncycle.\nAn example for the implementation of a\nara::exec::WorkerRunnable\ncan be\nfound in [10].\nThe aim is to abstract the data processing as far as possible, irrespective of the ac-\ntual number of available threads.       "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nNormalizedInstruction\n= runtime in sec * clock frequency in Hz\nNormalizedInstruction\ndoes not reflect the actual number of code instructions,\nbut allows the description of comparative resource needs.\nThe following parameters (\nDeterministicClientResource\n, see\n[TPS_MANI_01200] in [3]) are relevant for describing the computing time bud-\nget needs of a\nprocess\nwhich uses\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::\nRunWorkerPool\n.\nThe parameters are needed to be specified twice per\nprocess\nwhich uses\nDe-\nterministicClient\n, once for the\nkInit\ncycle and once for the\nkRun\ncycles\n(\nDeterministicClientResourceNeeds\n, and [TPS_MANI_01199]).\n•\nnumberOfInstructions\n[NormalizedInstructions]\nThis is the normalized runtime consumption on the target system within one cy-\ncle, assuming the worst-case runtime where the workers would be executed\nsequentially.\n•\nspeedup\n= sequental runtime / parallelized runtime\nDefines how much faster the calculations within one cycle can be finished if\nnum-\nberOfWorkers\n(see 7.6.3.2) are physically available, i.e. if enough cores were\navailable on the machine to perform parallel execution of all workers.\n•\nsequentialInstructionsBegin\n[NormalizedInstructions]\nThis is the normalized sequential runtime at the beginning of the cycle (which\nmostly cannot be parallelized), before the main usage of the worker pool starts.\n•\nsequentialInstructionsEnd\n[NormalizedInstructions]\nThis is the normalized sequential runtime at the end of the cycle (which mostly\ncannot be parallelized), after the main usage of the worker pool has ended.\nExamples\nExample 7.5\nThe\nprocess\nuses the worker pool mainly in the middle of the cycle.       "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.21: Full utilization of worker pool\n7.6.4 Deterministic Synchronization\nThe API\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\nis de-\nscribed in 7.6.3 as the wait point in deterministic redundant execution. In this sec-\ntion, more details on synchronization behaviors will be provided for both periodic and\nevent-triggered activation in the execution cycles.\n7.6.4.1 DeterministicSyncMaster\nA\nDeterministicSyncMaster\n[TPS_MANI_01406] is a synchronization control\npoint that receives the synchronization requests through a dedicated communication\nchannel, for example\nara::com\n, and sends the calculated cycle information for the\nnext execution cycle to the connected\nDeterministicClient\ns in the same domain.\nNote that it is not limited to use\nara::com\nor API of other communication channel,\nand it is up to the vendor to decide which to use. This specification only describes\nthe integration with\nara::com\nAPI for\nDeterministicSyncMaster\n. The integration\nwith other communication APIs is not covered and may be specified in a later release.\nFigure 7.22 shows an example of how a\nDeterministicSyncMaster\ncontrols the\nsynchronization for two\nDeterministicClient\ns of the application\nprocess\nbased\non\nara::com\ninterface for request and response communication.\n91 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.22: Sequence Diagram of the Synchronization Control Messages with single\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nFor event-triggered activation, a specific policy of the synchronization should be pro-\nvided. The policy is highly dependent on vendor solution and requirements, for ex-\nample, the synchronization response is sent to the\nDeterministicClient\ns only if\nthe synchronization requests from all the\nprocesses\nare received. There can be more\ncomplicated policies, e.g. the match of 2 out of 3 synchronization requests are received\nbefore the given deadline, which is also known as the M-out-of-N (MooN) policy.\nFor periodic activation, the\nDeterministicClient\ns require a single synchroniza-\ntion for the first\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\ncall\nthat is initiated after the execution of\nkInit\nor\nkServiceDiscovery\ncycle (see\n[SWS_EM_01304] for service modification). The activation response includes a global\ntime stamp for the activation of the first\nkRun\ncycle, which should also give a reason-\nable time buffer for receiving the activation response for the\nDeterministicClient\ns\nthrough the channel. All\nDeterministicClient\ns will count on local time until the\nactivation time is reached and then starts\nkRun\n. Further calls of\nara::exec::De-\nterministicClient::WaitForActivation\nwill not send any synchronization re-\nquest, but just return when the predefined deadline that was configured with\ncycle-\nTimeValue\nproperty is reached by the local time counter (see [SWS_EM_01351]).\nThe handling of missed deadline in the\nkRun\ncycles for periodic activation is described\nin [SWS_EM_01352].\nFor both periodic and event-triggered activation, a set of parameters need to be defined\nbefore the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nstarts.\n[SWS_EM_01320]\n{OBSOLETE}\nNumber of\nDeterministicClient\ns\n⌈\nThe number\nof\nDeterministicClient\ns that are connected to the\nDeterministicSyncMas-\nter\nshall be defined by attribute\nnumberOfConnectedClients\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00050,\nRS_EM_00051, RS_EM_00053)\n92 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 93,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n[SWS_EM_01321]\n{OBSOLETE}\nMinimum number of required synchronization re-\nquests\n⌈\nThe attribute\nminimumNumberOfRequests\nshall define the minimum num-\nber of required synchronization requests (from the connected\nDeterministic-\nClient\ns in the same domain) that are necessary to be received by the\nDetermin-\nisticSyncMaster\nto continue calculation of the next cycle.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00050, RS_-\nEM_00053)\nThe MooN policy defines a rule for\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nto decide when it\nshould respond to the synchronization requests for next execution cycle.\nN\nis the\nnumber of the\nprocesses\nthat are connected to the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nin the same domain ([SWS_EM_01320]), and\nM\nis the minimum required synchroniza-\ntion requests to be received in the same domain ([SWS_EM_01321]). The usage of\nMooN can be modified based on the requirements of the redundant execution. For\nexample, when\nM\nrequests are received (\nM < N\n), the\nDeterministicSyncMas-\nter\nmay ignore the rest of the unreceived requests, and start calculating the cycle\ninformation for the next activation based on the received requests. The cycle informa-\ntion is encapsulated into a response message and propagated to all of the connected\nDeterministicClient\ns. If\nM\nequals\nN\n, this means all of the requests from\nN\nDeterministicClient\ns should be received before proceeding to the calculation of\nnext cycle .\nNote that for the current release only MooN policy is described and the configuration\nof other policies may be specified in a later release.\n[SWS_EM_01322]\n{OBSOLETE}\nCalculation of the next cycle\n⌈\nIf\nverification-\nMethod\nis set to\nDeterministicSyncMOutOfN\n,\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nshall calculate the next activation time based on the MooN policy and the received\nsynchronization request. The MooN policy shall use the attribute\nnumberOfConnect-\nedClients\nas N and the attribute\nminimumNumberOfRequests\nas M. The received\nsynchronization request is used as the current valid input (see [SWS_EM_01325]).\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00050, RS_EM_00053)\nThe calculated cycle information is sent via a response message to all connected\nDe-\nterministicClient\ns (see [SWS_EM_01326]). Based on the response message,\na\nDeterministicClient\ntriggers the next execution cycle on the activation time by\nreturning from the\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\ncall.\n[SWS_EM_01323]\n{OBSOLETE}\nTotal\nkRun\nloop count\n⌈\nIf\nmaxRunCycleLoop\nis\nconfigured not to be zero,\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActi-\nvation\n(of the referencing\nDeterministicClient\n) shall return\nkTerminate\n, after\nkRun\nhas been returned\nmaxRunCycleLoop\ntimes\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00053)\n[SWS_EM_01324]\n{OBSOLETE}\nInfinite\nkRun\nloop\n⌈\nOmission of\nmaxRunCycleLoop\nconfiguration or a setting of zero shall indicate an infinite\nkRun\ncycle count.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00053)\nNote: The data type for storing the\nkRun\nloop count is implementation specific.\n93 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P94_176",

      "source_page": 94,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nThe current specification of\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nsupports redundant deter-\nministic execution in single domain. Multiple domains are not part of current specifica-\ntion. The\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nacts as a Time Slave [TPS_MANI_01409], in\norder to receive the global time stamp when it is needed for calculating and distribut-\ning the deterministic time stamps of execution cycles. The\nprocesses\nimplemented\nwith\nDeterministicClient\ns should be in the same global time domain as the\nDe-\nterministicSyncMaster\n, so they can be synchronized even if they are connected\nthrough network or gateway.\nFor single domain synchronization, both\nDeterministicClient\nand\nDeterminis-\nticSyncMaster\ncan use the local time resource for simplicity and efficiency when\nacquiring the current time. The access of the local time can be achieved by calling\nara::core::SteadyClock\nor, for example, the\nstd::chrono\nAPIs.\nThe assurance of secure access to the Time Resource should be managed by the Pol-\nicy Decision Point (PDP) and Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) configurations for Time\nSlave and Master. For example an Access Manager may be able to grant the per-\nmission for\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nto access the configured Time Master and\nTime Resource. As the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nexposes only\nara::com\nand\nara::tsync\ninterfaces, access control to functions of the\nDeterministicSync-\nMaster\nshould be enforced using IAM for\nara::com\nand\nara::tsync\n.\nWhen the\nprocess\nis running in the execution cycles, each cycle needs to be\nsynchronized by calling\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActi-\nvation\n. The behaviors to synchronize the\nprocess\nand the redundancies should\nbe performed by the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\n, which can be deployed in Execu-\ntion Management\nprocess\n, Software Lockstep\nprocess\nor in a separate\nprocess\n.\nFigure 7.23 shows an example of running the\nDeterministicSyncMaster\nin a sep-\narate\nprocess\n."

For example the Software Lockstep may\nalso need to understand the state of each execution cycle, in order to give more reason-\nable and trusty comparison results. Figure 7.24 gives examples of a Software Lockstep\nframework in library mode and\nprocess\nmode. Details of Software Lockstep will be\nspecified in a later release."

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n[SWS_EM_01325]\n{OBSOLETE}\nSynchronization Request Message\n⌈\nThe\nara::\nexec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\nfor a\nDeterministic-\nClient\nactivation shall send a synchronization request message to the connected\nDeterministicSyncMaster\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00050, RS_EM_00051, RS_EM_00053)\nA synchronization request should contain at least the following data members:\n•\nIdentification\n: the request needs to provide a unique identification.\n•\nActivation timestamp of the previous cycle\n: the activation of the previous cycle\nis used for calculate the next cycle.\n•\nCode of the current cycle\n: the type of the current cycle is used to determine the\ntype of next execution cycle. Possible codes are\nkServiceDiscovery\n,\nkInit\n,\nkRun\n.\n•\nCount of the current loop\n: the number of the execution loop is used to\ndetermine when\nara::exec::DeterministicClient::WaitForActiva-\ntion\nshould return\nkTerminate\n.\nThe concrete structure of the synchronization request/response messages, including\nthe data types of the members, is platform specific. Additionally, the interface mech-\nanism is between two platform specific elements and therefore also platform specific.\nIn case the interface between DeterministicClient and DeterministicSyncMaster is real-\nized using ara::com communication, the required identification could be a combination\nof the service instance ID of the service skeleton in the DeterministicClient/Determin-\nisticSyncMaster sending the message and the instance ID of the sending process.\n[SWS_EM_01326]\n{OBSOLETE}\nSynchronization Response Message\n⌈\nA\nDeter-\nministicSyncMaster\nshall send a synchronization response message to all the\nconnected\nDeterministicClient\ns when the applied synchronization policy is\nmatched.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00050, RS_EM_00051, RS_EM_00053)\nA synchronization response should contain at least the following data members:\n•\nIdentification\n: the request needs to provide a unique identification.\n•\nActivation timestamp for the next cycle\n: The calculated activation timestamp\nof the next execution cycle.\n•\nCode of the next cycle\n: The determined code of the next cycle. Possi-\nble values are\nkRun\n,\nkServiceDiscovery\n, and\nkTerminate\n. A\nkSer-\nviceDiscovery\ncode is returned when a service modification is necessary (see\n[SWS_EM_01304]). The code\nkTerminate\nindicates the termination of the de-\nterministic client and is returned when the total\nkRun\nloop count is reached or the\ntermination is requested by Execution Management (see [SWS_EM_01404]).\nAs for the request message, the concrete structure, including the data types of the\nmembers, of the response message is platform specific.\n[SWS_EM_01327]\n{OBSOLETE}\nReturn of the wait point API\n⌈\nA\nara::exec::\nDeterministicClient::WaitForActivation\ncall shall not return until the local\n96 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n7.7 Resource Limitation\nDespite the correct behavior of a particular\nAdaptive Application\nin the system,\nit is important to ensure any potentially incorrect behavior, as well as any unforeseen\ninteractions cannot cause interference in unrelated parts of the system [RS_SAF_-\n10008][11]. As\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\nalso strives to allow consolidation of\nseveral functions on the same machine, ensuring Freedom From Interference is a key\nproperty to maintain.\nHowever,\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\ncannot support all mechanisms as de-\nscribed in this overview chapter in a standardized way, because the availability highly\ndepends on the used Operating System.\nIn addition, it is important to consider that\nExecution Management\nis only respon-\nsible for the correct configuration of the\nMachine\n. However, enforcing the associated\nrestrictions is usually done by either the\nOperating System\nor another\nApplica-\ntion\nlike the Persistency service.\nSome mechanisms that could be standardized will not yet be defined in this release.\n7.7.1 Resource Configuration\nThis section provides an overview on resource assignment to\nModelled Processes\n.\nThe resources considered in this specification are:\n•\nRAM (e.g. for code, data, thread stacks, heap)\n•\nCPU time\nOther resources like persistent storage or I/O usage are also relevant, but are currently\nout of scope for this specification.\nIn general, we need to distinguish between two resource demand values:\n•\nMinimum resources, which need to be guaranteed so the process can reach its\nRunning state and perform its basic functionality.\n•\nMaximum resources, which might be temporarily needed and shall not be ex-\nceeded at any time, otherwise an error can be assumed.\nThe following stakeholders are involved in resource management:\n•\nApplication Developer\nThe Application developer should know how much memory (RAM) and comput-\ning resources the\nModelled Processes\nneed to perform their tasks within a\nspecific time. This needs to be specified in the Application description (which\ncan be the pre-integration stage of the\nExecution Manifest\n) which is handed\nover to the integrator. Additional constraints like a deadline for finishing a specific\ntask, e.g. cycle time, will usually also be configured here.\n98 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nHowever, the exact requirements may depend on the specific use case, e.g.\n\nThe RAM consumption might depend on the intended use, e.g. a video filter\nmight be configurable for different video resolutions, so the resource needs\nmight vary within a range.\n\nThe computing power required depends on the processor type. i.e. the re-\nsource demands need to be converted into a computing time on that specific\nhardware. Possible parallel thread execution on different cores also needs\nto be considered here.\nTherefore, while the Application developer should be able to bring estimates re-\ngarding the resource consumption, a precise usage cannot be provided out of\ncontext.\n•\nIntegrator\nThe integrator knows the specific platform and its available resources and con-\nstraints, as well as other applications which may run at the same time as the\nModelled Processes\nto be configured. The integrator should assign avail-\nable resources to the applications which can be active at the same time, which\nis closely related to\nState Management\nconfiguration, see section 7.5. If not\nenough resources are available at any given time to fulfill the maximum resource\nneeds of all running\nModelled Processes\n, assuming they are actually used\nby the\nModelled Processes\n, several steps have to be considered:\n\nAssignment of resource criticality to\nModelled Processes\n, depending on\nsafety and functional requirements.\n\nDepending on the Operating System, maximum resources which cannot be\nexceeded by design (e.g. Linux cgroups) can be assigned to a process or a\ngroup of\nprocesses\n.\n\nA scheduling policy has to be applied, so threads of\nprocesses\nwith high\ncriticality get guaranteed computing time and finish before a given deadline,\nwhile threads of less critical\nprocesses\nmight not. For details see section\n7.7.3.1.\n\nIf the summarized maximum RAM needs of all\nprocesses\n, which can be\nrunning in parallel at any given time, exceeds the available RAM, this cannot\nbe solved easily by prioritization, since memory assignment to low critical\nprocesses\ncannot just be removed without compromising the\nprocess\n.\nHowever, it should be ensured that\nprocesses\nwith high criticality have\nready access to their maximum resources at any time, while lower criticality\nprocesses\nneed to share the remaining resources. For details see 7.7.3.4.\nBased on the above, all the resource configuration elements are to be configured dur-\ning platform integration, most probably by the Integrator. To group these configuration\nelements, we define a\nResourceGroup\n. It may have several properties configured\n99 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nto enable restricting\nApplications\nrunning in the group. Subsequently, each\nMod-\nelled Process\nis required to belong to a\nResourceGroup\n, clarifying how the\nAp-\nplication\nwill be constrained at the system level.\n[SWS_EM_02102] Memory control\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall use\nRe-\nsourceGroup\n.\nmemUsage\nto configure the maximum amount of RAM available for\nall\nprocesses\nin the\nResourceGroup\nbefore loading any\nprocess\nfrom the\nRe-\nsourceGroup\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00005)\nIf a\nResourceGroup\ndoes not have a configured RAM limit, then the\nprocesses\nare\nonly bound by their implicit memory limit.\n[SWS_EM_02103] CPU usage control\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall use\nRe-\nsourceGroup\n.\ncpuUsage\nto configure the maximum amount of CPU time available\nfor all\nprocesses\nin each\nResourceGroup\nbefore loading any\nprocess\nfrom the\nResourceGroup\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00005)\nIf\nResourceGroup\ndoes not have a configured CPU usage limit, then the processes\nare only bound by their implicit CPU usage limit (priority, scheduling scheme...).\nBecause scheduling is done in very different ways depending on the\nOperating\nSystem\n, the specific algorithm for scheduling as well as limiting the CPU usage is\nnot described [SWS_OSI_02002].\nThe intention of\nResourceGroup\nis that limits are never reached and the\nResource-\nGroup\nlimits shall be configured by the integrator, based on measurement, not worst-\ncase execution time.\n7.7.2 Resource Monitoring\nAs far as technically possible, the resources which are actually used by a\nprocess\nshould be controlled at any given time. For the entire system, the monitoring part of\nthis activity is fulfilled by the Operating System. For details on CPU time monitoring\nsee 7.7.3.1. For RAM monitoring see 7.7.3.4. The monitoring capabilities depend on\nthe used Operating System. Depending on system requirements and safety goals,\nan appropriate Operating System has to be chosen and configured accordingly, in\ncombination with other monitoring mechanisms (e.g. for execution deadlines) which\nare provided by\nPlatform Health Management\n.\nResource monitoring can serve several purposes, e.g.\n•\nDetection of misbehavior of the monitored\nprocess\nto maintain the provided\nfunctionality and guarantee functional safety.\n•\nProtection of other parts of the system by isolating the erroneous\nprocesses\nfrom unaffected ones to avoid resource shortage.\nFor\nprocesses\nwhich are attempting to exceed their configured maximum resource\nneeds (see 7.7.1), one of the following alternatives is valid:\n100 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 101,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n•\nThe resource limit violation is considered as a failure and recovery actions may\nneed to be initiated. Therefore the specific violation gets reported to the\nState\nManagement\n, which then starts recovery actions.\n•\nIf the OS provides a way to limit resource consumption of a\nprocess\nor a group\nof\nprocesses\nby design, explicit external monitoring is usually not necessary\nand often not even possible. Instead, the limitation mechanisms make sure that\nresource availability for other parts of the system is not affected by failures within\nthe enclosed\nprocesses\n. When such by-design limitation is used, monitoring\nmechanisms may still be used for the benefit of the platform, but are not re-\nquired. Self-monitoring and out-of-process monitoring is currently out-of-scope in\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\n.\n7.7.3 Application-level Resource Configuration\nWe need to be able to configure minimum, guaranteed resources (RAM, computing\ntime) and maximum resources. In case Time or Full Determinism is required, the\nmaximum resource needs are guaranteed.\n7.7.3.1 CPU Usage\nCPU usage is represented in a process by its threads. Generally speaking,\nOperat-\ning System\ns use some properties of each thread's configuration to determine when\nto run it, and additionally constrain a group of threads to not use more than a defined\namount of CPU time. Because threads may be created at runtime, only the first thread\ncan be configured by\nExecution Management\n.\n7.7.3.2 Core Affinity\n[SWS_EM_02104] Core affinity\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall configure the Core\naffinity of the\nprocess\ninitial thread (restricting it to a sub-set of cores in the sys-\ntem) based on the configuration\nProcessToMachineMapping\n.\nshallRunOn\nand\nProcessToMachineMapping\n.\nshallNotRunOn\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00008)\nRequirement [SWS_EM_02104] permits the initial thread (the main thread of the pro-\ncess) to be bound to certain cores [SWS_OSI_01012]. Depending on the capabilities\nof the\nOperating System\nthe sub-set could be a single core. If the\nOperating\nSystem\ndoes not support binding to specific cores then the only supported sub-set is\nthe entire set of cores.\n101 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n7.7.3.3 Scheduling\nCurrently available POSIX compliant\nOperating System\ns offer the scheduling poli-\ncies required by POSIX, and in most cases additional, but different and incompatible\nscheduling strategies. This means for now, the required scheduling properties need to\nbe configured individually, depending on the chosen OS.\nMoreover, scheduling strategy is defined per thread and the POSIX standard al-\nlows for modifying the scheduling policy at runtime for a given thread, using\npthread_setschedparam()\n. It is therefore not currently possible for the\nAUTOSAR\nAdaptive Platform\nto enforce a particular scheduling strategy for an entire pro-\ncess, but only for its first thread.\n[SWS_EM_01014] Scheduling policy\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall configure the\nprocess scheduling policy (when launching a\nprocess\n) based on the relevant config-\nuration\nStartupConfig\n.\nschedulingPolicy\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00002)\nFor the detailed definitions of these policies, refer to [12]. Note,\nSCHED_OTHER\nshall be\ntreated as non real-time scheduling policy, and actual behavior of the policy is imple-\nmentation specific. It should not be assumed that the scheduling behavior is compatible\nbetween different\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\nimplementations, except that it is\na non real-time scheduling policy in a given implementation.\n•\n[SWS_EM_01041] Scheduling FIFO\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall be able\nto configure FIFO scheduling using policy\nSCHED_FIFO\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00002)\n•\n[SWS_EM_01042] Scheduling Round-Robin\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall\nbe able to configure round-robin scheduling using policy\nSCHED_RR\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00002)\n•\n[SWS_EM_01043] Scheduling Other\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall be able\nto configure non real-time scheduling using policy\nSCHED_OTHER\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00002)\nNote that the Scheduling Policies specified here are the minimal set. Depending on the\nOS there may be more Scheduling Policies configurable.\nWhile scheduling policies are not a sufficient method to guarantee Full Determinism,\nthey contribute to improve it. While the aim is to limit CPU time for a process, schedul-\ning policies apply to threads.\nNote that while\nExecution Management\nwill ensure the proper configuration for the\nfirst thread (that calls the\nmain()\nfunction), it is the responsibility of the\nprocess\nitself\nto properly configure secondary threads.\n[SWS_EM_01015] Scheduling priority\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall support the\nconfiguration of a scheduling priority when launching a\nprocess\nbased on the relevant\nconfiguration\nStartupConfig\n.\nschedulingPriority\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00002)\n102 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

    {
      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P103_185",
      "source_element": "SWS_EM_02108",
      "source_document": "AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement",
      "source_page": 103,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nThe available priority range and actual meaning of the scheduling priority depends\non the selected scheduling policy, see [constr_1692], [TPS_MANI_01061] and [TPS_-\nMANI_01188] in [3].\n7.7.3.3.1 Resource Management\nIn general, for deterministic behavior the required computing time is guaranteed and\nviolations are treated as errors, while best-effort subsystems are more robust and might\nbe able to mitigate sporadic violations, e.g. by continuing the calculation at the next\nactivation, or by providing a result of lesser quality. This means, if time (e.g. deadline\nor runtime budget) monitoring is in place, the reaction on deviations is different for\ndeterministic and best-effort subsystems.\nIn fact, it may not even be necessary to monitor best-effort subsystems, since they by\ndefinition are doing only a function that may not succeed. This leads to an architecture\nwhere monitoring is an optional property.\nThe remaining critical property however is to guarantee that a particular process or set\nof processes cannot adversely affect the behavior of other processes.\nTo guarantee Full Determinism for the entire system, it is important to ensure Free-\ndom From Interference, which the\nResourceGroup\ncontribute to ensure through the\noptional partitioning of available CPU and memory for the processes mapped to the\ngroup [SWS_EM_02108].\n[SWS_EM_02106] ResourceGroup assignment\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall\nconfigure the\nprocess\naccording to its\nResourceGroup\nmembership.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00005)\n7.7.3.4 Memory Budget and Monitoring\nprocesses\nrequire memory for their execution (e.g. code, data, heap, thread stacks).\nOver the course of its execution however, not all of this memory is required at all times,\nsuch that an OS can take advantage of this property to make these ranges of memory\navailable on-demand, and provide them to other\nprocesses\nwhen the memory is no\nlonger used.\nWhile this has clear advantages in terms of system flexibility as well as memory effi-\nciency, it is also in the way of both Time Determinism and Full Determinism: when a\nrange of memory that was previously unused should now be made available, the OS\nmay have to execute some amounts of potentially-unbounded activities to make this\nmemory available. Often, the reverse may also be happening, removing previously\navailable (but unused) memory from the\nprocess\nunder scope, to make it available to\nother\nprocesses\n. This is detrimental to an overall system determinism.\n103 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"
    },
    {
      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P104_186",
      "source_element": "SWS_EM_02108",
      "source_document": "AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement",
      "source_page": 104,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nExecution Management\nshould ensure that the entire memory range that determin-\nistic\nprocesses\nmay be using is available at the start and for the whole duration of the\nrespective\nprocess\nexecution.\nApplications not configured to be deterministic may be mapped on-demand.\nIn order to provide sufficient memory at the beginning of the execution of a\nprocess\n,\nsome properties may need to be defined for each\nprocess\n.\n[SWS_EM_02108] Maximum memory usage\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall con-\nfigure the Maximum memory usage of the\nprocess\naccording to the configuration\nitem\nProcess\n.\nstateDependentStartupConfig\n.\nresourceConsumption\n.\nmemo-\nryUsage\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00005)"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.27: Memory Usage.\nThe\nresourceConsumption\n.\nmemoryUsage\nis the amount of memory which can be\nallocated by the\nprocess\nitself. Please be aware, depending on the OS and its con-\nfiguration this does not necessarily contain all the memory the process can allocate\nwithin the system. For example in an OS where common functionality like a file system\nis implemented on process level, the restricted\nprocess\nmight still lead to memory\nallocations within the\nprocess\nproviding the file system.\nOn POSIX OS the memory limit is typically restricted by the resource RLIMIT_AS.\n[SWS_EM_02109] process pre-mapping\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall pre-map\na\nprocess\nif\nProcess\n.\npreMapping\nis set to true.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00005)\nFully pre-mapping a\nModelled Process\nensures that code and data execution is\nnot going to be delayed at its first execution by demand-loading. This helps providing\nTime Determinism during system startup and first execution phases, but also helps\n104 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

In addition, pre-mapping avoids late issues where filesystem may be\ncorrupted and part of the\nModelled Process\nmay not be loadable anymore.\n7.7.3.5 Working Folder\nThe working folder of a process is not defined by configuration but rather is deliberately\nleft as an implementation-specific element. The required PSE51 POSIX profile does\nnot define that an (Adaptive)\nApplication\nmay use the path or file argument for any\nfunction using a file pathname (e.g.,\nopen\n), instead only to specify the name of the\nobject without any file system semantics implied.\nThe PSE51 POSIX profile does not require the existence of a file system. Conse-\nquently, paths in\nAdaptive Applications\nmerely identify objects (e.g. in calls\nto\nopen()\nor\nstat()\n). The usage of sub-parts of a given path (e.g. \"\n/data\n\" when\n\"\n/data/config.dat\n\" was given) is implementation-defined.\n105 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P106_189",

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n7.8 Fault Tolerance\n7.8.1 Introduction\nWhat is Fault-Tolerance?\nThe method of coping with faults within a large-scale software system is termed fault\ntolerance.\nThe model adopted for\nExecution Management\nis outlined in [13].\nThis section provides context to the application of fault tolerance concepts with respect\nto\nExecution Management\nand perspective on how this contributes in overall plat-\nform instance's dependability.\nPlatform-wide Service Oriented Architecture fault tolerance aspects are outside the\nscope of this document and are not further addressed.\n7.8.2 Scope\nExecution Management\nhas a crucial influence on overall system behavior of the\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\n.\nThe effect of erroneous functionality, within\nExecution Management\ncan have very\ndifferent severity depending on operational mode and fault type. For example, a fault\nidentified by\nExecution Management\nmay have a local effect, influencing an inde-\npendent process only, or may become a root cause for a\nMachine\nwide failure.\nIt is therefore necessary not to specify only correct behavior but also to introduce alter-\nnative behavior in case of deviations.\nSuch mechanisms address a broad spectrum of concerns that emerge during\nMa-\nchine\nand\nprocess\nLife Cycle Management.\nThe\nAUTOSAR Adaptive Platform\narchitecture is composed of two levels;\nAppli-\ncation\nand\nPlatform Instance\n. The\nApplication\nlevel constitutes cooperative\nApplications\nintended to satisfy overall system's needs and objectives and repre-\nsents a service level in vehicle context. The\nPlatform Instance\nlevel as a reusable\nasset providing basic capabilities and platform level services. Fault tolerance within\nExecution Management\nis therefore required to handle both levels.\n7.8.3 Threat Model\nThe main threats which leading to incorrect behavior of software - whether\nAppli-\ncation\nor\nPlatform Instance\n- is the presence of systematic defects or faults\ni.e. those incorporated during design phase and remaining dormant untill deployment.\nOther sources of faults include physical faults, e.g. random hardware failures, that\n106 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 107,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nmight influence resource allocation and correct execution, and interraction faults which\ncan be a source for incorrect state transition requests."

      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P107_191",
      "source_element": "SWS_EM_02032",

      "source_page": 107,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.28: General Fault Tolerance scheme.\nFrom the perspective of\nExecution Management\n, fault activation occures when re-\nsulting\nFunction Group State\nor combination of such is requested. Due to the\ndifferent nature of faults, these can lead to various types of deviations from expected\nfunctional behavior and finally result in erroneous system functionality either in terms\nof correct computational results or timing response.\nIn general, the implementation of fault tolerance mechanism is based on two consistent\nsteps -\nError Detection\nand subsequent\nError Recovery\n. The major focus of\nError Detection\nduring\nDesign Phase\nactivities and thus the focus of\nFault\nTolerance\nin this specification is on the analysis of potential\nFailure Modes\nand\nthe consequent error detection mechanisms that should later be incorporated into the\nimplementation.\nIn contrast,\nError Recovery\nconsists of actions that should be taken in order to\nrestore the system's state where the system can once again perform correct service\ndelivery. Binding of\nError Detection\nand\nRecovery Actions\nshould be a subject\nof platform wide fault tolerance model.\nRemark:\nThe remainder of this section is the subject for elaboration for the next release\nof this specification. Provision for fault-tolerance mechanisms will consider possible\nfaults, how they can lead to errors within\nExecution Management\nand the mecha-\nnisms that are introduced to ensure error detection.\n7.8.4 Execution Management internal Error handling\nFrom System design point of view it is useful to have an\nExecution Management\n/OS\ninternal\nUnrecoverable State\n, which can be entered by\nExecution Manage-\nment\nwhen it has no other course of action. The\nUnrecoverable State\nis only\ntriggered by\nExecution Management\n.\n[SWS_EM_02032] On entry to the\nUnrecoverable State\n,\n⌈\nExecution Man-\nagement\nshall invoke a pre-cleanup action.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00150)\n[SWS_EM_02033] After execution of the pre-cleanup action,\n⌈\nall\nprocesses\nman-\naged by\nExecution Management\nshall be shutdown.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00150)\n107 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 108,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n[SWS_EM_02034] After all\nprocesses\nmanaged by\nExecution Management\nter-\nminated,\n⌈\na post-cleanup action shall be called.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00150)\nThe mechanism for invoking pre- and post-cleanup function is Platform specific. There\nis no requirement on which actions should be taken at each stage.\nIt is not possible to give an exhaustive of list of when the\nUnrecoverable State\nis entered. Potential examples when the\nUnrecoverable State\nshould be entered\ninclude:\n•\nThe underlying OS is not functioning as expected  for example failure of\nSIGKILL\n(i.e.\nExecution Management\ncannot kill processes).\n•\nExecution Management\nhas lost the ability to read the processed manifest,\ni.e. nothing can be started / stopped.\n•\nExecution Management\ncannot deliver responses (i.e. result of the requested\nFunction Group\nstate transitions) to\nState Management\n. Essentially\nExe-\ncution Management\nwill never respond back to SM for technical reasons.\n•\nTrusted platform configuration cannot be read meaning\nExecution Manage-\nment\ndoes not know it should run in a\nstrictMode\nor\nmonitorMode\n.\nNote:\nUnrecoverable State\nshould not be entered if\nExecution Management\ncan normally communicate with\nState Management\n in this case it is\nState Man-\nagement\n's responsibility to handle system errors (i.e. failed startup attempts).\n108 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 109,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n7.9 Security\n7.9.1 Trusted Platform\nFrom a security perspective, it is essential that all software executed on the Adaptive\nPlatform is trusted, i.e. the integrity and authenticity of the software is ensured.\nExecution Management\n- as the entity responsible for\nprocess\ncreation - has to\ntake over this task.\nA key requirement for a trusted Adaptive Platform is a Trust Anchor on the\nMachine\nthat is authentic by definition (hence that alternative name, \"root of trust\"). A Trust\nAnchor is often realized as a public key stored in a secure environment, e.g. in non-\nmodifiable persistent memory or in an HSM. The trust has to be passed to\nExecution\nManagement\nby appropriate means, e.g. by a chain of trust. If the\nMachine\ndoes not\nexhibit a Trust Anchor, it cannot be ensured that the Adaptive Platform is trusted.\n[SWS_EM_02299] Availability of a Trust Anchor\n⌈\nIf there is no Trust Anchor avail-\nable on the\nMachine\n, the following requirements may be ignored: [SWS_EM_02300],\n[SWS_EM_02301], [SWS_EM_02302], [SWS_EM_02303], [SWS_EM_02305],\n[SWS_EM_02306], [SWS_EM_02307], [SWS_EM_02308], [SWS_EM_02309].\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014)\nThere are many ways to verify the integrity and authenticity of the Adaptive Platform.\nA\nTrusted Platform\ncan be realized e.g. (but not limited to) by\n•\nVerification of the complete Ramdisk by the Bootloader\n•\nVerification of individual\nExecutables\nand data files, e.g. using OS-\nfunctionalities or a trusted third-party process\n•\nVerification of individual memory pages upon being loaded, e.g. using OS-\nfunctionalities or a trusted third-party process\n[SWS_EM_02300] Integrity and Authenticity of Machine configuration\n⌈\nExecu-\ntion Management\nshall ensure that the integrity and authenticity of Machine informa-\ntion from the processed\nManifests\nare checked before use.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_-\nEM_00015)\n[SWS_EM_02301] Integrity and Authenticity of each\nExecutable\n⌈\nExecution\nManagement\nshall ensure that for every\nprocess\nthat is about to be started, the in-\ntegrity and authenticity of the\nExecutable\nitself are checked.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_-\nEM_00015)\n[SWS_EM_02302] Integrity and Authenticity of shared objects\n⌈\nExecution Man-\nagement\nshall ensure that for every\nprocess\nthat is about to be started, the integrity\nand authenticity of each related shared object are checked.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_-\nEM_00015)\n[SWS_EM_02303] Integrity and Authenticity of processed\nExecution Manifest\nconfigurations\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall ensure that for every\nprocess\nthat\n109 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"
    },
    {
      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P110_194",
      "source_element": "SWS_EM_02303",
      "source_document": "AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement",
      "source_page": 110,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nis about to be started, the integrity and authenticity of its corresponding processed\nManifests\nare checked.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_EM_00015)\nThe information validated by [SWS_EM_02303] includes all manifest information, e.g.\nService Instance information, and not just the information directly used by\nExecution\nManagement\n.\nFrom a security perspective, the rationale for choosing these items is as follows:\n•\nExecutables\n: Modifying the Executable itself allows an attacker to execute ar-\nbitrary code on the machine;\n•\nManifests:\nMachine Manifests\n,\nExecution Manifests\nand\nService\nInstance Manifests\ndescribe what and how something should be executed\nand are thus an obvious attack vector on the Adaptive Platform;\n•\nShared Objects: Shared objects can either contain code that is executed within\nthe context of the\nprocess\nor data that (potentially) influences the execution of\na\nprocess\naccessing this data. A modified shared object could consequently be\nused to compromise the system.\nIn order to establish a\nTrusted Platform\n, it must be ensured that only trusted soft-\nware is launched. Therefore, a system designer has to ensure that\nExecution Man-\nagement\nis started authentically. For instance, this could be realized by a chain of trust\nas described in [14].\nExecution Management\nin turn has to ensure that all\nExecutable\ncode on the\nAdaptive Platform is authenticated before being executed. The complete authenticated\nstart-up sequence looks like this:\n110 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Figure 7.29: Authenticated start-up sequence\nThe integrity and authenticity of persistent data stored by applications is not considered\nhere. The\nFunctional Cluster\nPersistency takes care of the integrity of this data.\n7.9.1.1 Handling of failed authenticity checks\nIf the integrity and authenticity has been verified successfully, the system has to con-\ntinue with its regular start-up process. If the integrity and authenticity check has failed,\nhowever,\nExecution Management\noffers a configuration option on how to proceed\nwith the start-up process.\n[SWS_EM_02305] Failed authenticity checks\n⌈\nExecution Management\nshall\nselect the trusted platform mode based on the value of\nMachine\n.\ntrustedPlat-\nformExecutableLaunchBehavior\n.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_EM_00015)\nThe configuration of the three modes is done via the\ntrustedPlatformExe-\ncutableLaunchBehavior\nattribute within the\nProcessed Manifest\n. The config-\nuration option is only allowed to be processed after the integrity and authenticity of the\nrelevant\nProcessed Manifest\nhas been verified.\nThese three modes of the\nMachine\n.\ntrustedPlatformExecutableLaunchBe-\nhavior\nare:\n111 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 112,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n•\nmonitorMode\n•\nnoTrustedPlatformSupport\n•\nstrictMode\n[SWS_EM_02306]\n{DRAFT}\nLaunch Behavior Validation\n⌈\nExecution Manage-\nment\nshall stop the start-up sequence of the Adaptive Platform if the integrity or au-\nthenticity check of the\nProcessed Manifest\ncontaining the\ntrustedPlatformEx-\necutableLaunchBehavior\nselection has failed and switch to the unrecoverable\nstate.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_EM_00015)\nThe integrity and authenticity check applies to all trusted platform modes; to do oth-\nerwise would leave the system open to attacks that maliciously corrupt the Manifest\ninformation. Reaction to a failure is limited as, by definition, no Adaptive Applications\nother than\nExecution Management\nare running and hence are restricted to imple-\nmentation defined actions such as OS-level logging.\n7.9.1.1.1 Monitor Mode\nIn\nmonitorMode\n, the integrity and authenticity checks are performed, but the start-up\nprocess is not affected. Hence, the Adaptive Platform starts up even if the file system\nhas been compromised.\n[SWS_EM_02556] Monitor Mode\n⌈\nIn\nmonitorMode\n, if a check ([SWS_EM_02300],\n[SWS_EM_02301], [SWS_EM_02302] and [SWS_EM_02303]) fails then\nExecution\nManagement\nshall log the failure and continue regular startup of the Adaptive Plat-\nform.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014, RS_EM_00015)\nmonitorMode\nis useful when the integrator wants the system to keep running, even if\nthe platform is not considered trusted. In this case, the integrator might use additional\nmeasures outside the scope of Adaptive AUTOSAR, like e.g. restricted key access\nwhen using an HSM that supports this feature.\nmonitorMode\nis also useful during development phase, when frequent changes on\nthe Adaptive Platform are performed and keeping the authentication tag (e.g. signa-\ntures) valid is a tedious task.\n7.9.1.1.2 Strict Mode\nIn\nstrictMode\n, the Adaptive Platform ensures that no\nprocesses\nare executed,\nwhere the integrity and authenticity of the corresponding\nExecutable\n, manifests or\nlinked library could not be verified.\n112 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "id": "SNIP_exec_AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_E_P113_198",
      "source_element": "SWS_EM_02307",
      "source_document": "AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement",
      "source_page": 113,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\n[SWS_EM_02307]\n{DRAFT}\nStrict Mode - Execution manifest\n⌈\nIn\nstrictMode\n,\nExecution Management\nshall not initiate the execution of an Executable if the in-\ntegrity or authenticity check of the corresponding processed\nExecution Manifest\nhas failed.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014)\n[SWS_EM_02308]\n{DRAFT}\nStrict Mode - Service Instance manifests\n⌈\nIn\nstrict-\nMode\n,\nExecution Management\nshall not initiate the execution of an Executable if the\nintegrity or authenticity check of at least one of the corresponding processed\nService\nInstance Manifests\nhas failed.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014)\n[SWS_EM_02309]\n{DRAFT}\nStrict Mode - Executables\n⌈\nIn\nstrictMode\n,\nExecu-\ntion Management\nshall start a\nprocess\nonly if the integrity and authenticity of the\ncorresponding\nExecutable\nwas successfully verified.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_00014)\nExecutable code can be provided by executables and by statically linked shared objects\nlinked by the executable.\nExecution Management\ncannot determine dynamically\nlinked shared objects and thus these needs to be validated through an alternative,\nimplementation specific, mechanism.\nExample: Consider an Adaptive Platform in\nstrictMode\n.\nExecution Management\nhas started several\nExecutables\nafter successfully verifying the integrity and authen-\nticity of the\nExecutable\n, its related shared objects and its processed\nExecution\nManifest\n. Now,\nExecution Management\nwants to start another\nExecutable\n,\nwhere the authenticity check has failed.\nExecution Management\ndoes not launch\nthis\nExecutable\n, because it is not trusted. The other\nExecutables\nthat passed the\nauthenticity check may however continue to run. When\nExecution Management\nat-\ntempts to start another\nExecutable\nit can be started as long as all authenticity checks\nare passed.\n7.9.2 Identity and Access Management\nFollowing the \"Principle of Least Privilege\", Identity and Access Management (IAM)\n[15] was introduced in the Adaptive Platform. IAM allows to assign permissions to\nMod-\nelled Processes\nfor accessing public Interfaces from Functional Clusters. Hence,\nModelled Processes\nhave to be identifiable during runtime in order to lookup and\nenforce permissions accordingly.\nExecution Management\nstarts\nprocesses\nbased on\nModelled Processes\n.\nHence\nExecution Management\nis able to maintain the association between the two.\nExecution Management\nsupports IAM by revealing information about this associ-\nation. This allows IAM to authenticate processes during runtime with the help of the\noperating system and\nExecution Management\n.\n[SWS_EM_02400] Properties of IAM-configuration assigned to processes\n⌈\nExe-\ncution Management\nshall associate the\nidentity\nof a specific\nModelled Process\nwith the identity of the corresponding\nprocess\nduring\nprocess\ncreation.\n⌋\n(RS_EM_-\n00111, RS_EM_00015)\n113 of 197 Document ID 721: AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement"

      "source_page": 114,
      "category": "architectural_role",
      "verbatim_text": "Specification of Execution Management\nAUTOSAR AP R23-11\nThe form of identity is implementation specifc but could, for example, be the process\nidentifier, a cryptographic token, user ID, etc.\nBased on implementation requirements,\nExecution Management\nmay expose inter-\nfaces that allow IAM to retrieve information about the association between\nprocess\nand\nModelled Process\nidentity.   "bisheriges_fragment": "<div class=\"ai module-guide\"><p class=\"ai-note\">Automatisch generierte Beschreibung, inhaltlich abgeleitet aus den referenzierten AUTOSAR-R25-11-Dokumenten (SWS-Spezifikation und begleitende Standarddokumente) — kein offizieller AUTOSAR-Text. Als Interpretation gekennzeichnete Aussagen sind Schlussfolgerungen aus den Quellen.</p><h3>Rolle & Verwendungszweck</h3><p>Das Modul <code>ara::exec</code> (Execution Management) ist die zentrale Instanz für die Prozesssteuerung, das Scheduling und das Zustandsmanagement auf der AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform. Es bildet das Bindeglied zwischen dem zugrundeliegenden POSIX-Betriebssystem und der modularen AUTOSAR-Laufzeitumgebung <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01001\">[SWS_EM_01001]</a>.</p><p>Die Kernaufgaben von <code>ara::exec</code> umfassen:</p><ul><li><strong>Prozesslebenszyklus-Steuerung:</strong> Deterministischer Start, Überwachung und geordnete Terminierung modellierter POSIX-Prozesse basierend auf Execution- und Machine-Manifesten.</li><li><strong>Zustandsverwaltung über Funktionsgruppen:</strong> Abbildung von Systemzuständen auf <code>FunctionGroups</code> (z. B. <code>MachineState</code> oder anwendungsspezifische Gruppen), deren Zustände (<code>FunctionGroupStates</code>) exakt festlegen, welche Prozesse aktiv sein müssen.</li><li><strong>Lebenszyklus-Handshake (ExecutionClient):</strong> Jeder gestartete Prozess muss seine erfolgreiche Initialisierung aktiv über den <code>ExecutionClient</code> an das Execution Management melden.</li><li><strong>Ressourcen- und Scheduling-Konfiguration:</strong> Zuweisung von Betriebssystem-Ressourcen (CPU-Affinität, Speichergrenzen via ResourceGroups) sowie Scheduling-Strategien (z. B. Echtzeit-Scheduling via <code>SCHED_FIFO</code> / <code>SCHED_RR</code>).</li><li><strong>Fehlererkennung und -wiederherstellung:</strong> Erkennung von Prozessabstürzen, Timeout-Verletzungen beim Hochfahren und Signalisierung von Fehlern an das State Management.</li></ul><h3>Architektur- und Schnittstellenverträge</h3><p>Die Schnittstellenarchitektur von <code>ara::exec</code> unterscheidet streng zwischen der Schnittstelle für reguläre Anwendungsprozesse (<code>ExecutionClient</code>) und den Steuer-Schnittstellen für privilegierte Plattform-Komponenten (<code>StateClient</code>):</p><ul><li><strong>ExecutionClient:</strong> Normale Adaptive Applications instanziieren den <code>ara::exec::ExecutionClient</code> <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02002\">[SWS_EM_02002]</a>. Sobald die anwendungseigene Initialisierung abgeschlossen ist und die Anwendung bereit für den Normalbetrieb ist, ruft sie <code>ReportExecutionState(ExecutionState::kRunning)</code> auf <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02003\">[SWS_EM_02003]</a>. Vor der regulären Beendigung nach Erhalt eines Terminierungssignals signalisiert sie analog <code>ReportExecutionState(ExecutionState::kTerminating)</code>.</li><li><strong>FunctionGroup und FunctionGroupState:</strong> Eine Funktionsgruppe bündelt eine Menge von Prozessen, die gemeinsam aktiviert oder deaktiviert werden <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02272\">[SWS_EM_02272]</a>. Jeder gültige Zustand wird durch ein <code>FunctionGroupState</code>-Objekt repräsentiert <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02273\">[SWS_EM_02273]</a>. Standardmäßig besitzt jede Funktionsgruppe die Zustände <code>Off</code>, <code>Verify</code> und <code>Terminate</code>.</li><li><strong>Zustandswechsel-Schnittstelle:</strong> Privilegierte Management-Applikationen (State Management) fordern Zustandsänderungen über <code>SetState()</code> an <a class=\"swsref\" href=\"https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02285\">[SWS_EM_02285]</a>. Dieser Aufruf liefert ein <code>ara::core::Future</code> zurück, das erst erfüllt wird, wenn alle für den Zielzustand erforderlichen Prozesse erfolgreich gestartet wurden bzw. abgelöste Prozesse terminiert sind.</li><li><strong>Betriebssystem-Interaktion:</strong> Execution Management startet Prozesse typischerweise als Kindprozesse via <code>fork()</code> / <code>execve()</code> und richtet Signal-Handler ein, um den Exit-Status über <code>waitpid()</code> zu überwachen.</li></ul><h3>Interaktionsfluss</h3><p>Der Interaktionsfluss verknüpft State Management, Execution Management und die einzelnen Anwendungsprozesse. Fordert das State Management einen Zustandswechsel an, berechnet das EM die Prozess-Differenzmenge, startet neue Prozesse und wartet auf deren <code>kRunning</code>-Rückmeldung. Beim Herunterfahren wird den Prozessen ein SIGTERM zugestellt, woraufhin diese geordnet terminieren.</p><div class=\"diagram\" id=\"diag-01\"><svg xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/2000/svg\" viewbox=\"0 0 Die wesentlichen Überwachungs- und Fehlerpfade umfassen:</p><ul><li><strong>Startup- und Termination-Timeouts:</strong> Meldet ein gestarteter Prozess innerhalb des im Manifest konfigurierten Zeitfensters nicht <code>kRunning</code>, wertet das EM dies als Startfehler. und zu PHM</h4><p>EM konfiguriert das Betriebssystem für Scheduling und Ressourcenmanagement, führt aber das Runtime-Scheduling nicht selbst aus. Für beaufsichtigte Prozesse informiert EM PHM über <code>kRunning</code>, Terminierungsbeginn und Prozessende; PHM verwendet diese Ereignisse zum Starten oder Stoppen der Supervision <a class="docref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_OperatingSystemInterface.pdf#nameddest=subsection.7.1.3">SWS Operating System Interface §7.1.3 „Scheduling Policies“</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01210">[SWS_EM_01210]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01211">[SWS_EM_01211]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01212">[SWS_EM_01212]</a>.</p><h4>Verhalten im Fehlerfall</h4>
<p><code>ExecutionClient::ReportExecutionState()</code> liefert ein <code>Result<void></code>. Ein nicht bestätigbarer Bericht wird als <code>ExecErrc::kNoCommunication</code> zurückgegeben; bei einem ungültigen Zustandsbericht als <code>ExecErrc::kInvalidTransition</code>. Für einen <code>kRunning</code>-Bericht fordert Execution Management konkret den Process State <code>Starting</code>; ein Aufruf durch einen Non-reporting Process ist eine <code>ReportExecutionStateViolation</code>. <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02003">[SWS_EM_02003]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02243">[SWS_EM_02243]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01403">[SWS_EM_01403]</a></p>
<p>Ein Self-terminating Process darf die Terminierung selbst mit <code>EXIT_SUCCESS</code> beginnen oder auf <code>SIGTERM</code> von Execution Management warten. Davon abzugrenzen ist eine Unexpected Termination, etwa wenn ein als nicht selbstterminierend konfigurierter Process ohne vorherige Anforderung endet oder bevor er <code>kRunning</code> gemeldet hat. Sie kann zugleich eine Abnormal Termination sein. Außerhalb eines durch <code>StateClient::SetState()</code> angeforderten Übergangs setzt Execution Management die zugehörige Function Group auf den Undefined Function Group State und ruft den <code>undefinedStateCallback</code> mit einem <code>ExecutionErrorEvent</code> auf. Das Event enthält den Prozessfehler und den Function-Group-Kontext; ein anschließendes <code>GetExecutionError()</code> liefert dieselbe Information. <a class="docref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=chapter.2">SWS Execution Management §2 „Acronyms and Abbreviations“</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01309">[SWS_EM_01309]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02542">[SWS_EM_02542]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02545">[SWS_EM_02545]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02546">[SWS_EM_02546]</a></p>

<p class="diagram-note">Die Sequenz zeigt den für eine Unexpected Termination außerhalb eines angeforderten Function-Group-Übergangs festgelegten Meldeweg. Nachdem der Fehler als <code>ExecutionErrorEvent</code> vorliegt, bestimmt die nicht von einem Update betroffene StateMachine den konfigurierten Folgezustand aus ihrer <code>ErrorRecoveryTable</code>. Quellen: <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01309">[SWS_EM_01309]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02542">[SWS_EM_02542]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_StateManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_SM_00601">[SWS_SM_00601]</a>.</p>
<p>Schlägt während eines Function-Group-Übergangs der Start eines Process fehl, beendet Execution Management den Übergang, setzt den Current State auf Undefined und meldet über das <code>SetState()</code>-Future <code>ExecErrc::kOperationFailed</code>; der konfigurierte <code>ExecutionError</code> ist über <code>GetExecutionError()</code> verfügbar. Bei Abnormal oder Unexpected Termination eines für den Requested State konfigurierten Process ist der korrespondierende Fehler <code>ExecErrc::kUnexpectedTermination</code>. Das <code>SetState()</code>-Future kann außerdem unter anderem <code>kOperationCanceled</code>, <code>kNoCommunication</code> oder <code>kInvalidTransition</code> enthalten; letzteres deckt verbotene oder ungültige Zielzustände ab. <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02259">[SWS_EM_02259]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02315">[SWS_EM_02315]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02278">[SWS_EM_02278]</a></p>

und zu PHM</h4><p>EM konfiguriert das Betriebssystem für Scheduling und Ressourcenmanagement, führt aber das Runtime-Scheduling nicht selbst aus. Für beaufsichtigte Prozesse informiert EM PHM über <code>kRunning</code>, Terminierungsbeginn und Prozessende; PHM verwendet diese Ereignisse zum Starten oder Stoppen der Supervision <a class="docref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_OperatingSystemInterface.pdf#nameddest=subsection.7.1.3">SWS Operating System Interface §7.1.3 „Scheduling Policies“</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01210">[SWS_EM_01210]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01211">[SWS_EM_01211]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01212">[SWS_EM_01212]</a>.</p><h4>Verhalten im Fehlerfall</h4> <p><code>ExecutionClient::ReportExecutionState()</code> liefert ein <code>Result<void></code>. Ein nicht bestätigbarer Bericht wird als <code>ExecErrc::kNoCommunication</code> zurückgegeben; bei einem ungültigen Zustandsbericht als <code>ExecErrc::kInvalidTransition</code>. Für einen <code>kRunning</code>-Bericht fordert Execution Management konkret den Process State <code>Starting</code>; ein Aufruf durch einen Non-reporting Process ist eine <code>ReportExecutionStateViolation</code>. <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02003">[SWS_EM_02003]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_02243">[SWS_EM_02243]</a> <a class="swsref" href="https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R25-11/AP/AUTOSAR_AP_SWS_ExecutionManagement.pdf#nameddest=SWS_EM_01403">[SWS_EM_01403]</a></p> <p>Ein Self-terminating Process darf die Terminierung selbst mit <code>EXIT_SUCCESS</code> beginnen oder auf <code>SIGTERM</code> von Execution Management warten. Davon abzugrenzen ist eine Unexpected Termination, etwa wenn ein als nicht selbstterminierend konfigurierter Process ohne vorherige Anforderung endet oder bevor er <code>kRunning</code> gemeldet hat. Sie kann zugleich eine Abnormal Termination sein. Außerhalb eines durch <code>StateClient::SetState()</code> angeforderten Übergangs setzt Execution Management die zugehörige Function Group auf den Undefined Function Group State und ruft den <code>undefinedStateCallback</code> mit einem <code>ExecutionErrorEvent</code> auf.
